meta.title: IPE knowledge network, c. 1976-2026
meta.description: Key works and theme nodes in top-journal International Political Economy, seeded from this repo's papers.json (Zotero) and supplemented with canonical works. Edges are typed relations with a one-line justification. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work); belongs_to edges link works to themes.

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

meta.verification: Repo works: from the user's Zotero library (papers.json). Supplementary works: each looked up in Crossref on 2026-10-28 by title and first author; result recorded in each node's `verified` field. One work (Colgan & Keohane 2017, Foreign Affairs) could not be confirmed in Crossref. Works added by the coverage audit take title, authors, year, venue and DOI directly from Crossref records; their claims are my summaries.

nodes.title: Political Cleavages and Changing Exposure to Trade
nodes.claim: Stolper-Samuelson plus a simple political model: trade expansion empowers owners of locally abundant factors and hurts scarce ones, so factor endowments predict whether trade shocks produce class or urban-rural coalitions.
nodes.method: Deductive theory with illustrative historical survey
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text; not an empirical study)

nodes.label: Rogowski 1987
nodes.title: Trade and the Variety of Democratic Institutions
nodes.claim: Trade-dependent democracies need insulated, stable, autonomous states, so they drift toward PR, large districts and parliamentarism.
nodes.method: OECD cross-section c. 1970, correlations and path analysis
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Hiscox 2001
nodes.title: Class Versus Industry Cleavages: Inter-Industry Factor Mobility and the Politics of Trade
nodes.claim: Whether trade politics pits classes or industries against each other depends on inter-industry factor mobility: high mobility yields Stolper-Samuelson class cleavages, low mobility yields Ricardo-Viner industry cleavages.
nodes.method: Historical wage/profit dispersion measures for six countries 1815-1994 with qualitative evidence
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Scheve 2001
nodes.authors: Kenneth F. Scheve & Matthew J. Slaughter
nodes.title: What Determines Individual Trade-Policy Preferences?
nodes.claim: Factor type, proxied by skill, predicts US trade preferences in line with Heckscher-Ohlin: low-skilled workers favor protection, and home ownership in import-competing counties adds an asset channel.
nodes.method: NES survey data, probit models
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Journal of International Economics, 2001; DOI 10.1016/s0022-1996(00)00094-5)

nodes.label: Mayda 2005
nodes.title: Why Are Some People (and Countries) More Protectionist Than Others?
nodes.claim: Across countries, skill raises support for trade in skill-abundant economies and lowers it in skill-scarce ones, consistent with factor endowments; but values, national pride and neighborhood attachment matter independently.
nodes.method: ISSP and WVS cross-national surveys
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2001, earlier working-paper version; DOI 10.3386/w8461)

nodes.label: Hainmueller 2006
nodes.title: Learning to Love Globalization: Education and Individual Attitudes toward International Trade
nodes.claim: The education effect on trade support reflects exposure to economic ideas and cosmopolitan values rather than labor-market skill: it holds for the retired and non-working, and tracks college exposure, not occupation.
nodes.method: ISSP and NES survey analysis
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2006; DOI 10.1017/s0020818306060140)

nodes.label: Mansfield 2009
nodes.authors: Edward D. Mansfield & Diana C. Mutz
nodes.title: Support for Free Trade: Self-Interest, Sociotropic Politics, and Out-Group Anxiety
nodes.claim: Trade attitudes are driven less by material self-interest than by sociotropic perceptions of national effects and by out-group anxiety; the education gradient largely reflects isolationism and ethnocentrism.
nodes.method: Two US national surveys with detailed occupation and industry items
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Rho 2017
nodes.title: Why Don't Trade Preferences Reflect Economic Self-Interest?
nodes.claim: Most people do not know how trade affects their own income; even when informed, many still weigh sociotropic and distributional concerns, so self-interest cannot anchor trade preferences.
nodes.method: US survey experiments with information treatments
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2017; DOI 10.1017/s0020818316000394)

nodes.label: Owen 2017
nodes.title: Occupation and the Political Economy of Trade: Job Routineness, Offshorability, and Protectionist Sentiment
nodes.claim: Workers in routine-task and offshorable occupations are more protectionist in rich democracies, reviving a material account at the level of occupational tasks rather than skill or industry.
nodes.method: ISSP 2003 and 2013 surveys across high-income democracies
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2017; DOI 10.1017/s0020818317000339); also web-verified

nodes.label: Mutz 2018
nodes.title: Status Threat, Not Economic Hardship, Explains the 2016 Presidential Vote
nodes.claim: Trump support tracked perceived threats to dominant-group status (including from China's rise and trade) rather than personal economic hardship.
nodes.method: US panel survey 2012-2016
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2018; DOI 10.1073/pnas.1718155115)

nodes.label: Ballard-Rosa 2024
nodes.authors: Cameron Ballard-Rosa, Judith Goldstein & Nita Rudra
nodes.title: Trade as Villain: Belief in the American Dream and Declining Support for Globalization
nodes.claim: Elite rhetoric that trade is unfair resonates most with meritocratic Americans who worry about their prospects; blaming foreign trade practices drives falling support for globalization.
nodes.method: Survey experiments plus an original panel
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Carnegie 2022
nodes.title: Public Opinion on Geopolitics and Trade: Theory and Evidence
nodes.claim: Affective beliefs about other countries shape trade preferences: people prefer trading with allies and resist adversaries, amplified by beliefs that trade strengthens rivals' militaries.
nodes.method: Survey experiments in the US and India, open-ended responses, case evidence
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Bisbee 2025
nodes.title: Antiglobalization Sentiment: Exposure and Immobility
nodes.claim: Antiglobalization sentiment rises where import exposure meets occupational immobility: workers whose jobs are dissimilar from local alternatives feel the most insecurity.
nodes.method: New individual exposure-by-immobility measure (O*NET) applied to US attitudes toward NAFTA
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Scheve 2024
nodes.title: Trains, Trade, and Transformation: A Spatial Rogowski Theory of America's 19th-Century Protectionism
nodes.claim: Falling transport costs enriched land-intensive exporters but drew protectionist migrant workers into farm regions, so trade's winners lost political power: a spatial twist on Rogowski.
nodes.method: County-level railroad expansion 1880-1900, votes and newspaper-based protectionist sentiment
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Pandya 2010
nodes.title: Labor Markets and the Demand for Foreign Direct Investment
nodes.claim: Support for inward FDI rises with skill because multinationals raise labor demand and skilled wages, shifting FDI research from investor supply to host-country demand.
nodes.method: Latinobarometer 1995-2001, probit with country fixed effects
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Ruggie 1982
nodes.title: International Regimes, Transactions, and Change: Embedded Liberalism in the Postwar Economic Order
nodes.claim: Postwar openness rested on a compromise fusing multilateral liberalization with domestic intervention for stability; regimes fuse power with legitimate social purpose, so hegemony predicts the form but not the content of order.
nodes.method: Historical-interpretive essay
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text; not an empirical study)

nodes.label: Cameron 1978
nodes.title: The Expansion of the Public Economy: A Comparative Analysis
nodes.claim: Trade openness is the strongest predictor of public-sector growth in rich democracies, via industrial concentration, unionization and left governments.
nodes.method: Cross-national OECD regressions 1960-1975
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (American Political Science Review, 1978; DOI 10.2307/1954537)

nodes.label: Rodrik 1998
nodes.title: Why Do More Open Economies Have Bigger Governments?
nodes.claim: Open economies have larger governments because public spending insures against external risk; the openness-government link is strongest where terms-of-trade volatility is high.
nodes.method: Cross-national regressions, 100+ countries
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 1996, earlier working-paper version; DOI 10.3386/w5537)

nodes.label: Garrett 1998
nodes.title: Partisan Politics in the Global Economy
nodes.claim: Globalization did not force convergence: where strong left parties and encompassing unions coexist, governments can sustain redistribution and still compete.
nodes.method: OECD panel analysis
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Cambridge University Press, 1998; DOI 10.1017/cbo9780511625633)

nodes.label: Adserà 2002
nodes.title: Trade, Democracy, and the Size of the Public Sector: The Political Underpinnings of Openness
nodes.claim: The openness-government link is political: in democracies exporters win free trade only by compensating exposed sectors; open economies with small states arise mainly under authoritarian rule.
nodes.method: Formal model and panel of ~65 countries 1950-1990
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Rudra 2002
nodes.title: Globalization and the Decline of the Welfare State in Less-Developed Countries
nodes.claim: In LDCs, surplus low-skilled labor cannot defend social spending as globalization deepens, so openness shrinks welfare where potential labor power is weak, reversing the OECD compensation pattern.
nodes.method: Panel of 53 LDCs 1972-1995 with a new potential-labor-power index
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Rudra 2005
nodes.title: Globalization and the Strengthening of Democracy in the Developing World
nodes.claim: Openness improves democracy in developing countries only when rising social spending compensates losers; otherwise elites choose repression.
nodes.method: Panel of 59 developing countries 1972-1997, FE and 2SLS
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Hays 2005
nodes.authors: Jude C. Hays, Sean D. Ehrlich & Clint Peinhardt
nodes.title: Government Spending and Public Support for Trade in the OECD: An Empirical Test of the Embedded Liberalism Thesis
nodes.claim: Where governments spend more on social protection and active labor-market policy, exposed workers are more supportive of trade: the micro-foundation of embedded liberalism.
nodes.method: ISSP survey data with country-level spending
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2005; DOI 10.1017/s0020818305050150)

nodes.label: Walter 2010
nodes.title: Globalization and the Welfare State: Testing the Microfoundations of the Compensation Hypothesis
nodes.claim: Globalization-exposed individuals feel more economic insecurity, which raises demand for welfare and, given it, support for openness: the compensation chain holds at the individual level.
nodes.method: Swiss survey data, structural models
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Studies Quarterly, 2010; DOI 10.1111/j.1468-2478.2010.00593.x)

nodes.label: Margalit 2011
nodes.title: Costly Jobs: Trade-Related Layoffs, Government Compensation, and Voting in U.S. Elections
nodes.claim: Trade-related job losses cost incumbents votes, more than other layoffs, but Trade Adjustment Assistance compensation measurably blunts the punishment.
nodes.method: County-level TAA certifications and presidential vote
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (American Political Science Review, 2011; DOI 10.1017/s000305541000050x)

nodes.label: Kim 2021
nodes.authors: Sung Eun Kim & Krzysztof J. Pelc
nodes.title: The Politics of Trade Adjustment Versus Trade Protection
nodes.claim: Counties with successful TAA petitions file fewer demands for trade protection: compensation and protection act as substitutes, and TAA yields Democratic electoral gains.
nodes.method: Geocoded antidumping petitions matched to TAA data
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Comparative Political Studies, 2020; DOI 10.1177/0010414020957687); also web-verified

nodes.label: Kim 2025
nodes.authors: In Song Kim, Megumi Naoi & Tomoya Sasaki
nodes.title: Domestic Institutions, Geographic Concentration, and Agricultural Liberalization
nodes.claim: Constitutions decide where the compensation contract is enforced: parliamentary systems liberalize and compensate geographically concentrated crops, presidential systems favor diffuse ones.
nodes.method: Product-level tariff cuts in 155 PTAs by 38 democracies 1995-2016, remote-sensed crop concentration
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text); authors/year web-verified

nodes.label: Zohlnhöfer 2018
nodes.authors: Reimut Zohlnhöfer, Fabian Engler & Kathrin Dümig
nodes.title: The Retreat of the Interventionist State in Advanced Democracies
nodes.claim: Government intervention has receded on almost every instrument since 1980 except social spending, and 130 quantitative studies disagree on why because of research-design choices, not settled nulls.
nodes.method: Systematic review of 130 studies plus OECD trend data
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text; not an empirical study)

nodes.label: Goodman 2021
nodes.authors: Sara Wallace Goodman & Thomas B. Pepinsky
nodes.title: The Exclusionary Foundations of Embedded Liberalism
nodes.claim: Embedded liberalism also depended on migration: receiving democracies combined open labor migration with generous welfare only by excluding migrants from rights; later inclusion eroded the compact from below.
nodes.method: Historical-institutionalist comparison of West Germany, UK and Japan
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Schneider 2024
nodes.title: Globalization and Promissory Representation
nodes.claim: Economic globalization lowers governing parties' pledge fulfillment through macro uncertainty and international constraints, a representational cost of interdependence.
nodes.method: 7,770 pledges across 12 countries, 1970s-2010s
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Baccini 2024
nodes.title: Austerity, Economic Vulnerability, and Populism
nodes.claim: Austerity raises populist support, but only among economically vulnerable voters; backlash is partly policy-made rather than only shock-driven.
nodes.method: District-level European elections since the 1990s, TWFE with vulnerability interactions
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text); year approximate (AJPS, c. 2024)

nodes.label: Autor 2013
nodes.authors: David H. Autor, David Dorn & Gordon H. Hanson
nodes.title: The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States
nodes.claim: Rising Chinese import competition explains a quarter of the US manufacturing employment decline 1990-2007 and raised transfer receipt and unemployment in exposed commuting zones.
nodes.method: Shift-share instrument using other rich countries' China imports
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2012; DOI 10.3386/w18054)

nodes.label: Autor 2020
nodes.authors: David Autor, David Dorn, Gordon Hanson & Kaveh Majlesi
nodes.title: Importing Political Polarization? The Electoral Consequences of Rising Trade Exposure
nodes.claim: China-shock exposure pushed US districts toward ideologically extreme representatives and raised Trump's 2016 vote share, mainly among white majorities.
nodes.method: Shift-share China shock on congressional and presidential outcomes
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2016, earlier working-paper version; DOI 10.3386/w22637)

nodes.label: Colantone 2018
nodes.title: The Trade Origins of Economic Nationalism: Import Competition and Voting Behavior in Western Europe
nodes.claim: Regions more exposed to Chinese imports shifted toward nationalist, isolationist and radical-right parties as the embedded-liberalism promise of compensation lost credibility.
nodes.method: 76 elections in 15 countries 1988-2007, shift-share China shock, ESS individual data
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Colantone 2018
nodes.title: Global Competition and Brexit
nodes.claim: Leave support was systematically higher in regions hit harder by the China import shock, and the effect ran through sociotropic rather than personal exposure.
nodes.method: Regional shift-share China shock and referendum results plus BES survey
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Elsevier BV, 2016, earlier working-paper version; DOI 10.2139/ssrn.2870313)

nodes.label: Jensen 2017
nodes.authors: J. Bradford Jensen, Dennis P. Quinn & Stephen Weymouth
nodes.title: Winners and Losers in International Trade: The Effects on US Presidential Voting
nodes.claim: Both losers and winners vote on trade: counties with import-competing low-skill manufacturing punish incumbents while counties with high-skill tradable services reward them.
nodes.method: County-level presidential votes 1992-2012 with industry trade exposure
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2016; DOI 10.3386/w21899)

nodes.label: Baccini 2021
nodes.title: Gone for Good: Deindustrialization, White Voter Backlash, and US Presidential Voting
nodes.claim: Long-run manufacturing job loss shifted white voters toward Republicans but Black voters toward Democrats, so deindustrialization's politics is racialized group-status politics, not uniform economic voting.
nodes.method: County and individual-level analysis 2000-2016
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (American Political Science Review, 2021; DOI 10.1017/s0003055421000022)

nodes.label: Ballard-Rosa 2021
nodes.authors: Cameron Ballard-Rosa, Mashail Malik, Stephanie Rickard & Kenneth Scheve
nodes.title: The Economic Origins of Authoritarian Values: Evidence from Local Trade Shocks in the United Kingdom
nodes.claim: Import-competition shocks raise authoritarian values among exposed individuals, a psychological mechanism linking economic shock to cultural backlash.
nodes.method: UK regional China shock matched to survey values
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Comparative Political Studies, 2021; DOI 10.1177/00104140211024296)

nodes.label: Rodrik 2018
nodes.title: Populism and the Economics of Globalization
nodes.claim: Advanced-stage globalization generates large distributional losses with small efficiency gains; whether backlash takes left (class) or right (identity) form depends on which cleavage is salient (trade/finance vs. immigration).
nodes.method: Synthetic essay with descriptive data
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2017; DOI 10.3386/w23559)

nodes.label: Rodrik 2021
nodes.title: Why Does Globalization Fuel Populism? Economics, Culture, and the Rise of Right-Wing Populism
nodes.claim: Four mechanisms connect globalization shocks to right-wing populism (direct, via cultural grievance, via political supply, via elite cues); evidence supports an economic root beneath cultural expression.
nodes.method: Literature synthesis
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2020; DOI 10.3386/w27526)

nodes.label: Walter 2021
nodes.title: The Backlash Against Globalization
nodes.claim: Backlash has three layers (attitudes, behavior, policy); evidence is strongest that economic and cultural drivers interact, and that elites and institutions decide whether grievance becomes policy reversal.
nodes.method: Literature synthesis
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Annual Review of Political Science, 2021; DOI 10.1146/annurev-polisci-041719-102405)

nodes.label: Margalit 2019
nodes.title: Economic Insecurity and the Causes of Populism, Reconsidered
nodes.claim: Economic shocks are 'outcome significant' but explain only a small share of populist support; cultural and partisan factors dominate the variance even where trade shocks have real effects.
nodes.method: Critical review of evidence
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019; DOI 10.1257/jep.33.4.152)

nodes.label: Norris 2019
nodes.title: Cultural Backlash: Trump, Brexit, and Authoritarian Populism
nodes.claim: Authoritarian populism is a reaction by older, less educated cohorts to generational value change toward post-materialism; economics matters mainly as an accelerant.
nodes.method: Cross-national survey and party data
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Cambridge University Press, 2019; DOI 10.1017/9781108595841)

nodes.label: Flaherty 2021
nodes.title: Rising Inequality as a Threat to the Liberal International Order
nodes.claim: Newer trade theories (superstar workers, firms, cities) predict top-heavy gains that classical factor models miss, so far more people lose from openness and backlash follows where top inequality is high.
nodes.method: Theoretical review plus re-analysis of two European datasets
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text); year 2021 (IO 75th-anniversary issue)

nodes.label: Broz 2021
nodes.authors: J. Lawrence Broz, Jeffry Frieden & Stephen Weymouth
nodes.title: Populism in Place: The Economic Geography of the Globalization Backlash
nodes.claim: Backlash is rooted in place: trade, offshoring and automation hollowed manufacturing towns whose decline spilled into property, services and health, while superstar cities thrived.
nodes.method: Descriptive US county and EU regional data plus county OLS for 2012-2016 swing
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text); year 2021 (IO 75th-anniversary issue)

nodes.label: Han 2024
nodes.title: The Deep Roots of American Populism
nodes.claim: 1890s People's Party strongholds vote populist today; globalization shocks catalyzed populism in both eras, and latent attitudes persisted in between.
nodes.method: County-level persistence with IV for 1890s globalization
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text); unpublished, year approximate

nodes.label: Kim 2021
nodes.title: Tariffs As Electoral Weapons: The Political Geography of the US-China Trade War
nodes.claim: China targeted retaliatory tariffs at Republican-leaning counties, and exposed voters shifted away from the GOP in 2018: trade policy as a tool of foreign electoral pressure.
nodes.method: Product-county exposure to Chinese retaliation and 2018 midterm results
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2021; DOI 10.1017/s0020818320000612)

nodes.label: Blanchard 2024
nodes.authors: Emily J. Blanchard, Chad P. Bown & Davin Chor
nodes.title: Did Trump's Trade War Impact the 2018 Election?
nodes.claim: Republican House candidates lost ground in counties exposed to foreign retaliatory tariffs and gained little from US protection; farm subsidies offset only modestly.
nodes.method: County-level tariff exposure and 2018 House results
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2019, earlier working-paper version; DOI 10.3386/w26434); also web-verified

nodes.label: Milner 2021
nodes.title: Is Global Capitalism Compatible with Democracy? Inequality, Insecurity, and Interdependence
nodes.claim: Globalization strains liberal democracy through three pathways: inequality undermines political equality, insecurity feeds populism, and interdependence constrains policy and shifts authority to IOs.
nodes.method: ISA presidential address synthesizing the literature
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text; not an empirical study)

nodes.label: Ahlquist 2020
nodes.authors: John Ahlquist, Mark Copelovitch & Stefanie Walter
nodes.title: The Political Consequences of External Economic Shocks: Evidence from Poland
nodes.claim: Voters directly hit by an external shock (Swiss-franc mortgages) form interest-consistent preferences and respond to targeted promises, while unexposed voters follow partisan cues.
nodes.method: Pre-election Polish survey with embedded experiment after the 2015 franc shock
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Melitz 2003
nodes.title: The Impact of Trade on Intra-Industry Reallocations and Aggregate Industry Productivity
nodes.claim: With heterogeneous firms, only the most productive export; liberalization reallocates market share within industries toward them. The economic foundation of firm-level trade politics.
nodes.method: Formal general-equilibrium model
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2002; DOI 10.3386/w8881)

nodes.label: Kim 2017
nodes.title: Political Cleavages within Industry: Firm-Level Lobbying for Trade Liberalization
nodes.claim: Most tariff variation is within industries: product differentiation frees productive exporters from collective-action problems, so they lobby individually for liberalization of their own products.
nodes.method: New firm-level Lobbying Disclosure Act dataset linked to product tariffs
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Osgood 2017
nodes.title: The Breakdown of Industrial Opposition to Trade: Firms, Product Variety, and Reciprocal Liberalization
nodes.claim: In differentiated-product industries, reciprocal liberalization splits firms within industries and large exporters dominate position-taking, dissolving industry-level opposition.
nodes.method: Original data on firm and association positions on 15 US trade agreements 1995-2012
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Osgood 2018
nodes.title: Globalizing the Supply Chain: Firm and Industrial Support for US Trade Agreements
nodes.claim: Firms that produce abroad or import intermediates are the core of the pro-trade coalition; direct import competition matters mainly in homogeneous-goods industries.
nodes.method: Positions of 403 industries across ten US FTAs with input-output offshoring measures
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Blanchard 2016
nodes.authors: Emily J. Blanchard, Chad P. Bown & Robert C. Johnson
nodes.title: Global Supply Chains and Trade Policy
nodes.claim: Governments set lower tariffs on goods whose value added comes from partner countries with which they share supply chains, so GVC integration disciplines protection.
nodes.method: Theory plus product-level tariff and value-added trade data
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2016; DOI 10.3386/w21883)

nodes.label: Baccini 2017
nodes.authors: Leonardo Baccini, Pablo M. Pinto & Stephen Weymouth
nodes.title: The Distributional Consequences of Preferential Trade Liberalization: Firm-Level Evidence
nodes.claim: PTAs raise sales and employment at large, productive, multinational-linked firms and hurt small domestic ones: the firm-level distributional footprint of trade agreements.
nodes.method: Firm-level data across many countries and PTAs
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2017; DOI 10.1017/s002081831700011x)

nodes.label: Kim 2019
nodes.authors: In Song Kim, Helen V. Milner, Thomas Bernauer, Iain Osgood, Gabriele Spilker & Dustin Tingley
nodes.title: Firms and Global Value Chains: Identifying Firms' Multidimensional Trade Preferences
nodes.claim: Firms' trade-policy priorities vary more by firm than industry: GVC multinationals prize investment protection, non-GVC exporters prize dispute settlement, tariffs matter less.
nodes.method: Conjoint experiment on firms in Costa Rica
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Kim 2019
nodes.title: Firms in Trade and Trade Politics
nodes.claim: Synthesizes the firm turn: heterogeneous firms, product differentiation and GVCs replace industries and factors as the units of trade politics, with implications for lobbying, agreements and backlash.
nodes.method: Literature review
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (Annual Review of Political Science, 2019; DOI 10.1146/annurev-polisci-050317-063728)

nodes.label: Zhang 2023
nodes.title: Commerce, Coalitions, and Global Value Chains: Coordinated and Collective Lobbying on Trade
nodes.claim: Firms linked through common foreign GVC partners lobby together and share lobbyists; relational supply-chain ties solve collective-action problems for small groups of large firms.
nodes.method: FactSet firm-to-firm supply-chain network 2003-2020 matched to lobbying reports
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Malesky 2018
nodes.title: Chains of Love? Global Production and the Firm-Level Diffusion of Labor Standards
nodes.claim: Supply chains diffuse labor standards upward only when the markup gap between high- and low-standard markets is large and lead firms care about labor practices.
nodes.method: Survey experiment on ~900 foreign-invested firms in Vietnam
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)

nodes.label: Kim 2025
nodes.authors: In Song Kim, Steven Liao & Sayumi Miyano
nodes.title: How FDI Reshapes Host Markets' Trade Profile and Politics
nodes.claim: Greenfield FDI widens host export profiles toward GVC products and creates new pro-liberalization coalitions, visible in deeper tariff cuts on FDI-linked products.
nodes.method: Global fDi Markets projects 2003-2017, Vietnamese customs records, DiD with matching
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text); authors/year web-verified

nodes.label: Jensen 2003
nodes.title: Democratic Governance and Multinational Corporations: Political Regimes and Inflows of Foreign Direct Investment
nodes.claim: Democracies attract more FDI because credibility and audience costs lower political risk, contrary to the view that autocracies offer investors a better deal.
nodes.method: Cross-national panel of FDI inflows
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (International Organization, 2003; DOI 10.1017/s0020818303573040)

nodes.label: Büthe 2008
nodes.title: The Politics of Foreign Direct Investment into Developing Countries: Increasing FDI through International Trade Agreements?
nodes.claim: GATT/WTO membership and PTAs raise FDI into developing countries by making liberal policy commitments credible.
nodes.method: Panel of 122 developing countries 1970-2000
nodes.verified: Crossref: title and author matched (American Journal of Political Science, 2008; DOI 10.1111/j.1540-5907.2008.00340.x)

nodes.label: Büthe 2014
nodes.title: Foreign Direct Investment and Institutional Diversity in Trade Agreements: Credibility, Commitment, and Economic Flows in the Developing World
nodes.claim: PTAs attract FDI through credibility, so ratified agreements with strict investment clauses and third-party dispute settlement draw more investment than signed or shallow ones.
nodes.method: Panel of 122 economies 1971-2007 with a new 385-PTA design dataset
nodes.verified: repo analysis (full text)
